Q: REST API PATCH without request body A:

Late to the party, but I didn't see any answer citing actual documentation or standards...

First off, an easy place to start is the Mozilla docs if you ever have a question like this, which state that for a PATCH, the request must contain a body.

If you don't want to be a chump and blindly trust the Mozilla docs though, check out §2 of RFC 5789, the standard proposing PATCH:

The PATCH method requests that a set of changes described in the

request entity be applied to the resource identified by the Request-

URI. The set of changes is represented in a format called a "patch

document" identified by a media type. If the Request-URI does not

point to an existing resource, the server MAY create a new resource,

depending on the patch document type (whether it can logically modify

a null resource) and permissions, etc.

A "request entity" is commonly defined in HTTP as the body of the request, as well as certain headers (headers which you should NOT set manually).

So yes, the PATCH request must contain a body.

Therefore, is it possible and not a bad practice to send no body to a PATCH method?

Is it possible? Absolutely. REST is just a collection of architectural styles / standards, you're free to send an HTTP request with anything you want to include on it; hell, you could even make up your own HTTP method to use if PATCH isn't doing it for you.

But just because you can, doesn't mean you should. For example, I can send a GET request with a body in Postman - the body will still be sent to the server. Setting up a basic TCP socket server in your favorite programming language and printing out the data received would show something like this:

GET /test HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8080
Content-Type: text/plain
User-Agent: PostmanRuntime/10.13.6
Accept: */*
Content-Length: 31

this is the body of the request

But, some HTTP libraries will just not include bodies on GET requests to the servers, even if they're explicitly added to the request to comply with REST standards (see this issue in fetch for an example).

TLDR; If you go with PATCH requests, include a request body. If you don't include one, YMMV - breaking standards is always a great way to shoot yourself in the foot down the line.

Q: How to get the padding position of a long double value in C++? A:

Intel long double with padding is simpler than it looks

The data item is at the front of the field and six slack bytes are after. Since this format is Intel-only, that means you have mantissa low..high followed by exponent low..high followed by slack bytes. I know because I dumped it all out

Q: Generating astronomically many strings A:

64-char is impossible. But for batch generation, absolutely DON'T use any loop or map-reduce-fold other than right at the beginning to make every 2-char combo, for instance.

From there on, always use regex to do "string-squaring". From 1 single call to regex and your 2-char combos will already become all 65,536 4-char combos. "string-square" that just 1 more time and you already have all 4.29 billion 8-char hex combinations, which would require 32 GB of RAM, at the very least. If you're ultra bored, then string-square it 3 more times.

8 chars —> string-squaring (SSq) —> 16 chars —> SSq —> 32 chars —> SSq —> 64 chars

Mind you though : 64 hex digits are 256-bit numbers.

And this is all only theoretical above 8-char combos, cuz most regex engines wouldn't let you create a replacement string that large so string-square it from that point on.

Q: Is there a secure way to upload AAB file without sharing keystore on Indus Appstore? A:

There is a secure way to achieve exactly what you want keeping your keystore private while still offering your users the optimized, smaller download sizes of an App Bundle.

Here are the two best ways to handle this on the Indus Appstore:

1. The Best Method: Upload an .apks File (APK Set Archive)

While the Indus Appstore asks for a keystore when you upload an .aab, they also support the .apks file format.

An .apks file is essentially a zipped archive containing all the device-specific split APKs that would normally be generated by the app store. By generating this file locally, you sign the app on your own machine, meaning your keystore never leaves your computer. When you upload the .apks to Indus, they simply distribute the pre-signed, optimized splits to users, preserving the small download size.

How to do it using Android bundletool:

  1. Build your .aab file as you normally do.

  2. Download bundletool (an open-source command-line tool by Google).

  3. Run the following command in your terminal to generate and sign the .apks file locally:

Bash

java -jar bundletool.jar build-apks \
--bundle=/path/to/your/app.aab \
--output=/path/to/your/app.apks \
--ks=/path/to/your/keystore.jks \
--ks-pass=pass:YOUR_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD \
--ks-key-alias=YOUR_ALIAS \
--key-pass=pass:YOUR_KEY_PASSWORD

Upload the resulting app.apks file to the Indus Appstore Developer Console OR via their developer api tool and github actions.

Q: Is there a way to upload the latest app version via CI on indusappstore? A:

Yes, it is possible to upload the latest version of an Android application to the Indus Appstore through a CI/CD pipeline without using the graphical interface. The platform provides developer APIs that allow developers to programmatically upload new APK or AAB files and update app versions directly from automated workflows. Similar to the publishing process available in the Google Play Console through the Google Play Developer API, the Indus Appstore allows authenticated API requests where developers can send a POST request to specific endpoints such as /Devtools/aab/upgrade/{package} for AAB files or /apk/upgrade/ for APK files. To use this system, developers must first generate an API token from the DevTools section of the Indus Appstore developer dashboard and store it securely in their CI environment variables. Once the application is built and properly signed within the pipeline, the CI tool can automatically upload the file using scripts or HTTP requests. This setup works with many CI/CD platforms such as GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab, or CircleCI. As a result, developers can fully automate their deployment workflow so that every successful build can be uploaded to the Indus Appstore without manual intervention, improving efficiency and ensuring faster release management.
